analysis.file_name: BofA - Global Energy Weekly - Oil turns blue - 5 Nov 2026.pdf
analysis.title: Global Energy Weekly: Oil turns blue
key_insights: Global oil supply disruptions hit a record in 2026, with about 18mn b/d offline at the peak, the largest in data going back to 1965. The IEA estimated more than 10mn b/d of Gulf production remained shut in during August.

The market entered the conflict well supplied after several quarters of surplus. Global stocks tracked weekly peaked at 6.0bn barrels in March and are being drawn down rapidly. The IEA estimated observed global inventories fell by 507mn barrels between February and August.

Global inventories fell at about 2.8mn b/d, while BofA estimates demand destruction exceeded 3mn b/d for much of the conflict. Floating storage is disappearing quickly, driven by extreme backwardation and high shipping costs.

Chinese commercial stocks are at very low seasonally adjusted levels, and BofA believes China has started to tap its strategic reserves. China crude imports fell from about 13mn b/d in December 2025 to a low of 7.5mn b/d in June, then rebounded somewhat.
OECD stocks fell from 1.2bn to 1.0bn barrels between January and the latest reading, about 1mn b/d. OECD government stocks drew 19mn barrels in August, which commercial builds more than offset.
The Brent curve is in steep backwardation. The front-over-third-month Brent premium peaked at $21/bbl. Dated Brent has traded at a steep premium to front-month contracts.

Long-dated crude prices have barely moved during the conflict, and WCS in Hardisty has not rallied much past marginal production cost. BofA reads this as the market expecting mean reversion to cost of production over 2 to 3 years. Prediction markets see no near-term resolution but more weight on a solution over 12-24 months.

Middle East crude exports through Hormuz recovered to an estimated 7.4mn b/d in September, but shipping incidents picked up in October. Middle East product exports have not recovered materially, so product markets are tighter than crude.

Russian product exports fell from 2.4mn b/d in 2025 to 1.1mn b/d in July after repeated Ukrainian strikes on refineries. IEA estimated August global refinery throughput at 81.4mn b/d, 4.2mn b/d lower year over year.

ICE gasoil cracks and global gasoline cracks remain exceptionally high, and Atlantic Basin refining margins hit records in August. BofA forecasts ICE gasoil cracks near $67/bbl in 3Q26 and $62/bbl in 4Q26, and calls diesel bullish through the rest of 2026 or until Hormuz flows normalize.
Shipping costs from deep in the Persian Gulf to Asia exceeded $60/bbl at times, and longer voyages have raised oil on water.

Demand has held up. The global composite PMI is 55 and US oil consumption is steady. Primary energy spending as a share of GDP and US energy spending as a share of disposable income remain below levels tied to past energy-driven recessions.

AI investment, a US budget deficit near 6% of GDP and strong nominal US growth support activity. The US is a large net energy exporter, and BofA estimates the war's net impact on US GDP has been positive so far. Economists forecast 3.4% world GDP growth for 2026, down 0.1 point from the start of the year.

Brent forecasts stay at $96 for 2H26 and $80 for 2027. A ceasefire in the US-Iran, Saudi-Houthi or Russia-Ukraine conflicts could push Brent toward $80 or lower. A 'neither war nor peace' scenario could hold Brent around $100. Renewed US-Iran conflict could push Brent toward $150 in 2027.
BofA expects a 3.4mn b/d oil deficit in 3Q26 turning into a 1.5mn b/d surplus by 4Q27, with 2026 demand loss of about 3.0mn b/d and 2027 demand growth of about 4.3mn b/d.

Other forecasts: Henry Hub averages $3.55/mmbtu in 2026 and $3.35 in 2027. TTF averages EUR63/MWh in 2026 and EUR55 in 2027. Newcastle coal averages $150/t in 2026 and $125/t in 2027. EUA could approach EUR100/t this winter.

sector_views.rationale: Supply disruptions in Russia, China and the Middle East keep products tight, and elevated prices are needed to stop inventories falling to critical lows.
Supply grows 3.8Bcf/d and demand 1.9Bcf/d in 2026, with LNG exports up 2.7Bcf/d. Forecasts are $3.55 in 2026 and $3.35 in 2027.
A strong El Niño and LNG constraints should keep prices supported despite easing Middle East tensions.

macro_indicators.interpretation: The report cites 3.1% for 2026 in Exhibit 1 and 3.4% in the text. Growth is only 0.1 point below the start-of-year projection, so the supply shock has not derailed activity.
Manufacturing and services PMIs are both in expansion, so demand is holding despite the supply shock.
The path depends on whether the US-Iran war ends. Peace points to $80 or lower, a stalemate to about $100, renewed conflict to $150.
Fiscal support is helping keep nominal US growth strong.

macro_indicators.reading: 3.4mn b/d deficit in 3Q26, 1.5mn b/d surplus by 4Q27
macro_indicators.interpretation: The market flips from deficit to surplus if supply normalizes.

risk_factors: Renewed US-Iran kinetic conflict with lower global inventories, less price-responsive US shale and limited short-run demand elasticity could push Brent toward $150 in 2027.
Depleted strategic stocks in the OECD and China leave little buffer against another supply shock.
Shipping incidents in October threaten the recovery in Hormuz flows.
Refinery outages in Russia and the Middle East keep product markets tight even if crude flows improve.
A fragile status quo with intermittent attacks, constrained Iranian supply and elevated shipping risk could keep Brent near triple digits in 2027.
Persistent high energy prices could eventually cause demand destruction or a recession, though energy spending shares are still below historical recession levels.
vol_and_positioning: Front-over-third-month Brent timespread peaked at $21/bbl, described as very rare.
Oil market volatility is sharply higher, and the Brent curve is in steep backwardation with Dated Brent at a steep premium to front month.
Gasoil and gasoline cracks are extremely elevated, and Atlantic Basin refining margins hit records in August.
geopolitical: US-Iran war and disruption through the Strait of Hormuz, with more than 10mn b/d of Gulf production shut in during August per the IEA.
Saudi-Houthi conflict and Red Sea routing, with Saudi Arabia sending nearly 4mn b/d through the East-West pipeline.
Russia-Ukraine conflict, with Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries cutting product exports.
Democratic midterm gains and whether they open the way to an Iran peace deal, which BofA says depends largely on President Trump.
Pickup in shipping incidents in October that puts Hormuz flows at risk.
US Navy arrangement to allow passage of barrels from the Persian Gulf.

tension_points.bull_case: A ceasefire in the US-Iran, Saudi-Houthi or Russia-Ukraine conflicts could unlock production, normalize trade routes and refinery use, and push Brent toward $80 or lower in 2027. Long-dated prices and prediction markets already point to normalization.
tension_points.bear_case: A 'neither war nor peace' stalemate keeps the physical market tight with Brent around $100, and renewed US-Iran conflict could push Brent toward $150 with depleted inventories and less responsive US shale.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A ceasefire or peace deal would invalidate the tight-market view. Renewed US-Iran kinetic conflict would invalidate the normalization view.

theme_stances.key_argument: Record supply disruption and depleted buffers leave the oil market more exposed to the next shock, so the US-Iran war remains central to oil prices.
Diesel outlook is bullish through 2026 or until Hormuz flows normalize because elevated prices are needed to prevent critically low inventories.
